Seeing Beyond the Frame

The story of my photography

Arpita Nath

A reflection

When I first picked up a camera, I wasn’t sure what I was really doing; I just went with instinct. I started taking pictures of things that were interesting, moments that got in the way of a pause, and scenes that I didn’t want to forget. I didn’t focus on meaning or technique. Through discussing photography and taking this course, my vision has changed, as it affects not only how I see what is in front of the lens, but also how I perceive the act of photographing. Photography is more than just pushing a button; it’s about making choices. I learned how composition, light, and timing shape a photo’s story. Techniques like framing, leading lines, and perspective became intentional tools in my work. Now, I think before I shoot, looking for shapes, shadows, and subtle movements that add depth beyond surface value.

Learning about Henri Cartier-Bresson greatly inspired me. His concept of “decisive moment” taught me to anticipate and appreciate the beauty in spontaneous moments. I used to take pictures quickly to avoid missing out, but now I slow down, observing how people move and how light shifts. His street photography has shown me that it’s the photographer’s role to see and respond to the world’s active moments. Robert Capa's blurry, jarring images were unexpectedly valuable to me as well. The grain, the blurry feelings, the rawness of it all were not improperly handled; they were authentic. This helped me to stop thinking of my images needing to be polished. My favourite images now are not perfect, but they have a feeling. Capa reminded me that photography isn't about being an accurate picture; photography sometimes is about impact. On another note, Ansel Adams helped me think more critically about editing and tonal range. While he is known for his landscape images, his thoughtfulness of light and contrast taught me how much editing is reflected in mood. I began to see how simple change—a highlight slightly more distracting, or a shadow made deeper—could alter the whole mood of a photo.

Beyond the multitude of graphical influences, this course also allowed me to play. For example, I began to use depth more purposefully; the simple addition of foreground elements provides some scale. I experimented with angles; shooting my subject from great heights or great depths would change the energy of the subject. I began to notice things like symmetry bring calm, imbalance adds tension. Even the use of negative space, I feel a new confidence, allowing quietness to speak for itself. Most importantly, I no longer take pictures just for the sake of documenting something. I take pictures to communicate something. Instead of taking reactions, every picture feels like a decision. I have become more purposeful—not only with the final image, but with the significance of that image.

This growth has not been instantaneous; it has gradually settled in—one step at a time—with each assignment, each photo critique, every picture that did not fully work but taught me something along the way. I have developed a keener eye and steadier hand, and a greater knowledge of what to preserve in a moment. Even though I know I am still in the process of learning, I feel more grounded than before. Photography is no longer just something I enjoy—it’s something I understand. And that understanding has made all the difference.
